```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(message = FALSE, warning = FALSE, fig.width = 8, fig.height = 5)
library(tidyverse)

# locate the raw data whether this file is knit from results/, scripts/drafts/, or the repo root
raw_path <- c('data/biomarker-raw.csv',
              '../data/biomarker-raw.csv',
              '../../data/biomarker-raw.csv') %>%
  keep(file.exists) %>%
  first()
stopifnot(!is.na(raw_path))
```

# Load raw data

Same parsing as `preprocessing.R`, but **without** any transformation, scaling, or trimming.

```{r load-raw}
# protein names / abbreviations
var_names <- read_csv(raw_path, col_names = F, n_max = 2,
                      col_select = -(1:2)) %>%
  t() %>%
  as_tibble() %>%
  rename(name = V1,
         abbreviation = V2) %>%
  na.omit()

# raw (untransformed) protein levels, one row per subject
biomarker_raw <- read_csv(raw_path, skip = 2, col_select = -2L, 
                          col_names = c('group', 'empty',
                                        pull(var_names, abbreviation), 'ados'),
                          na = c('-', '')) %>%
  filter(!is.na(group)) %>%
  mutate(subject = row_number(), .before = 1) %>%
  select(subject, group, ados, everything())

protein_cols <- setdiff(names(biomarker_raw), c('subject', 'group', 'ados'))

tibble(subjects = nrow(biomarker_raw),
       proteins = length(protein_cols),
       missing_values = sum(is.na(biomarker_raw[protein_cols])),
       nonpositive_values = sum(biomarker_raw[protein_cols] <= 0, 
                                na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  knitr::kable()

biomarker_raw %>% count(group) %>% knitr::kable()
```

# 1.  What do you imagine is the reason for log-transforming the protein levels in `biomarker-raw.csv`? (Hint: look at the distribution of the raw values for a sample of proteins.)

Looking at the distribution of raw values for a sample of proteins...

## Raw vs. log distributions for a random sample of proteins

```{r sample-proteins}
set.seed(123)
sample_proteins <- sample(protein_cols, 6)

sample_long <- biomarker_raw %>%
  select(subject, group, all_of(sample_proteins)) %>%
  pivot_longer(-c(subject, group), names_to = 'protein', values_to = 'raw') %>%
  mutate(log10 = log10(raw))
```

```{r hist-raw}
ggplot(sample_long, aes(x = raw)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = 'darkblue', color = 'white') +
  facet_wrap(~ protein, scales = 'free') +
  labs(title = 'Raw protein levels (6 random proteins)', x = 'raw level', 
       y = 'count') +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r hist-log}
ggplot(sample_long, aes(x = log10)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = 'orangered', color = 'white') +
  facet_wrap(~ protein, scales = 'free') +
  labs(title = 'log protein levels (same 6 proteins)', x = 'log(level)', 
       y = 'count') +
  theme_minimal()
```

## Skewness across all proteins

```{r skewness}
skew <- function(x) {
  x <- x[!is.na(x)]
  mean((x - mean(x))^3) / (mean((x - mean(x))^2))^1.5
}

skew_tbl <- tibble(protein = protein_cols,
                   raw = map_dbl(protein_cols, ~ skew(biomarker_raw[[.x]])),
                   log10 = map_dbl(protein_cols, ~ 
                                     skew(log10(biomarker_raw[[.x]]))))

skew_tbl %>%
  pivot_longer(-protein, names_to = 'scale', values_to = 'skewness') %>%
  group_by(scale) %>%
  summarize(median_skew = median(skewness),
            pct_skew_gt_1 = 100 * mean(skewness > 1),
            pct_abs_skew_lt_0.5 = 100 * mean(abs(skewness) < 0.5)) %>%
  knitr::kable(digits = 2)

skew_tbl %>%
  pivot_longer(-protein, names_to = 'scale', values_to = 'skewness') %>%
  mutate(scale = factor(scale, levels = c('raw', 'log10'))) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = skewness, fill = scale)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 50, position = 'identity', alpha = 0.6, 
                 color = 'white') +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = 'dashed') +
  labs(title = paste0('Skewness of each protein (', length(protein_cols), 
                      ' proteins), before and after log10'),
       x = 'sample skewness', y = 'number of proteins') +
  theme_minimal()
```

## Scale differences between proteins

```{r scale-range}
protein_medians <- tibble(protein = protein_cols,
                          median_raw = map_dbl(protein_cols,
                                               ~ median(biomarker_raw[[.x]], 
                                                        na.rm = TRUE)))

ggplot(protein_medians, aes(x = median_raw)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 40, fill = 'grey40', color = 'white') +
  scale_x_log10() +
  labs(title = 'Median raw level of each protein (log-scaled x axis)',
       x = 'median raw level', y = 'number of proteins') +
  theme_minimal()
```


## Major Takeaways

```{r task1-numbers, include=FALSE}
med_raw  <- median(skew_tbl$raw)
med_log  <- median(skew_tbl$log10)
pct_raw  <- 100 * mean(skew_tbl$raw > 1)
pct_log  <- 100 * mean(skew_tbl$log10 > 1)
```

Raw protein levels are strongly right-skewed: the median skewness across proteins is `r round(med_raw, 2)` on the raw scale vs. `r round(med_log, 2)` after a log transform, and `r round(pct_raw)`% of proteins have skewness above 1 on the raw scale vs. `r round(pct_log)`% after the transform. 

A handful of very large values dominate each raw distribution. This is typical of concentration/intensity measurements, where variation is multiplicative (e.g., a fold change) rather than additive. Taking logs turns multiplicative variation into additive variation and pulls in the long right tail, which suits the methods used downstream (t-tests, which assume roughly normal data; logistic regression; and standardization, where the mean and SD would otherwise be inflated by a few extreme values). Proteins also differ in typical level by several orders of magnitude, so a common scale is needed before they can be compared or used jointly, which is handled by centering and scaling.

The log transform does not remove the skew entirely: a sizable share of proteins still have skewness above 1 on the log scale.
